vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: lobstercash
Version: 0.0.10

The skill bundle provides an interface for the Lobster Cash CLI (by Crossmint) to enable agent-led crypto payments, virtual card management, and cloud browser automation. While the documentation (SKILL.md and references/) includes extensive security guardrails—such as mandatory human-in-the-loop (HITL) approvals for all transactions, server-side credential handling via 'fill-card' to prevent LLM exposure, and live-view URLs for transparency—the skill inherently grants high-risk capabilities. These include the ability to spend user funds and control a remote browser session. Per the instructions, these risky capabilities are plausibly needed for the stated purpose but qualify as 'suspicious' due to their high-impact nature, despite the lack of evidence of malicious intent.

llm.summary: The skill's instructions largely match a payment/checkout tool, but it asks users to install and update an external npm package and relies on server-side handling of sensitive payment credentials — a combination that warrants caution before installing or using.

dimensions.detail: The name/description (spending, cards, crypto, checkout, browser automation) aligns with the runtime instructions: requesting virtual cards, sending crypto, browser automation, x402 payments, and signing transactions. Nothing requested in the skill (no env vars, no odd config paths) is obviously unrelated to payments. However, the skill requires installing an external npm CLI (@crossmint/lobster-cli) and contacting lobster.cash URLs to update, which is outside the registry's install mechanism and deserves scrutiny as part of the capability.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: The SKILL.md instructs the agent to run a third-party global npm install/update, open external approval URLs, and use server-side browser automation that can fill payment forms. It also supports two ways to get card credentials: a server-side 'fill-card' (credentials never reach the agent) and a 'cards reveal' that returns full card numbers/CVC to the CLI/agent. Revealing credentials to an agent is sensitive and could be abused if the agent is compromised or misused. The document mostly enforces human approval, but the ability to reveal credentials and to auto-install/upate from external URLs is broad and needs user trust/verification.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no install spec in the registry; the README tells users to run `npm install -g @crossmint/lobster-cli` and to update from https://www.lobster.cash/install when required. That directs installing/overwriting global binaries from the public npm registry and an external URL — both are higher-risk operations because they run arbitrary third-party code outside the skill sandbox.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill declares no required env vars or credentials, which is proportionate. It does reference an optional LOBSTER_AGENT_ID and server-side dashboards, and the workflow clearly relies on the vendor's servers for storing payment methods and handling card fills. That is expected for a payment service but means users must trust the external service with sensitive financial data.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill is not force-included (always: false). It allows normal autonomous invocation (default), which is expected for skills but increases blast radius when the skill can make payments or reveal card credentials. Combine that with the external install/update behavior and server-side handling of cards, and you should treat autonomous invocation as a meaningful risk if you enable it without restrictions.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: This skill appears to be what it claims (a checkout + wallet CLI) but has actions that require trust in an external service and running third‑party code. Before installing or enabling it: 1) Verify the publisher and the npm package (@crossmint/lobster-cli) and the domain (lobster.cash) are legitimate and trustworthy for handling payments. 2) Prefer not to run global npm installs from unknown packages; inspect the package source (e.g., GitHub repo, npm page) first. 3) Understand the difference between server-side card filling (credentials kept on vendor servers) and 'cards reveal' (returns full card number/CVC to the agent/CLI) — avoid using 'cards reveal' unless you fully trust the service and the agent session. 4) If you allow autonomous agent invocation, restrict or monitor it because the agent can initiate payment flows; require explicit human confirmation for any write/payment action. 5) If you want higher assurance, ask the skill author for provenance (source repo, signed releases) or prefer an officially vetted integration with a known provider. If you want, I can summarize the specific risky commands and prompts to look for or draft a checklist to validate the npm package and vendor.
